rv.q: Harbour gives a tender and hilarious performance. The supporting cast is excellent, too. [It] boldly cracks open the suffocating messiness of death, family, and mental health.
Rebeck's gloriously off-the-wall drama has soul in spades, and feeds her leading men with one-liners to relish.

Instead this is an evening distinguished by its two lead performances: Pullman, painfully and defiantly nasty; Harbour superb as Michael — a gentle bear of a man haunted by his own fragilities and ill-suited to a tough, grasping world.
With its pacey first half and the acting of Henry and the two male leads, Mad House holds your attention.
It's still a thought-provoking piece, but you're left wondering what might have been.
It is ultimately a play with bits of brilliance, aspiring for the power and reach of an Arthur Miller or Eugene O'Neill drama but falling – heroically – short.

Director Moritz von Stuelpnagel keeps things pacy, and secures fine, flamboyant performances from this A-grade cast. But still, this is all deeply old-fashioned stuff which ... could have easily been written any time in the last five decades.

'Mad House' has an absolutely tremendous cast who were never not going to be able to carry this off. But ultimately you're left with a play that doesn't know if it wants to be 'Hamlet' or 'Clybourne Park', and suffers as a result.
Something of a halfway-house hit, then.
Rebeck's script suffers from its low stakes and ponderous pace.
The dark humour, realistically emotional storyline and top tier acting from the entire cast combine to create a must-see show.
There is some terrific acting, a few great lines and moments of fitful brilliance. But the overall package fails to deliver.
It's a memorable vehicle for David Harbour's talent, and that is a compelling reason in itself to see this show.
Despite the light touch of the hard-working cast, the play's over-inflated highs and lows are like eating a meal of sugary food: It provides a rush, but leaves you unsatisfied.

The world premiere of Theresa Rebeck's latest play is set in Pennsylvania where Michael has returned to his family home to look after his dying father, following a spell in hospital to look after his own mental health.
Theresa Rebeck's Mad House is theatrical brilliance, a story we can all identify with, but beautifully told and elevated by complex characters.
